utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the registrar would call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-95-14/1-A, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances, please. The Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I'm Upawansa Yapa and I appear for the Prosecutor with Mr. William Fenrick and Mr. Norman Farrell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. For the appellant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Srdzan Joka, Defence counsel for the accused Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is the appeal of Zlatko Aleksovski against the judgement and sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber in this case. It will be heard together with an appeal by the Prosecutor, a cross-appeal, also against the judgement and sentence. The appellant's notice, the accused's notice was, in fact, filed first in this case and therefore we propose to hear his appeal first. We will hear the Prosecution in reply. There will be a right of the appellant to respond briefly to that. Thereafter, we will hear the Prosecution appeal and then the appellant in reply. Unless there are any objections, that is the course which we propose to follow. But I would add this, that there have been voluminous written pleadings in this case and there is no need for counsel to repeat them. What we want to hear today is fresh argument and clarification of matters which may not be clear from the pleadings. The timetable which we will follow is to sit from now until 11. We'll then adjourn for half an hour. We will sit from 11.30 to 1 and there will then be the luncheon adjournment. We will sit again then from half past two to four. By this time, we hope to have concluded the hearing, but if we haven't, there will be the possibility of extending the hearing. Now, unless there are any objections, I propose to turn to the appellant's case. Mr. Joka, I propose to summarise the grounds of appeal as I understand them. If I have any of them wrong, would you kindly say so and explain what the ground is to us so that we have it fully in mind. But as I understand the position, the first ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber failed to establish that the accused had a discriminatory intent which you say is necessary to convict him for the offences under Article 3 of the Statute. The second ground, as I understand it, is that the conduct proved, in particular, the violence against the detainees, was not sufficiently grave as to warrant a conviction under Article 3 and, secondly, that it may have been justified by necessity. Pausing there, that is, in effect, two grounds, and I would add this, that we asked for additional briefs on the issue of necessity and, Mr. Joka, you said that you would expand, you're prepared to expand your brief in argument and, indeed, we shall invite you to do that. The third ground is that the Trial Chamber erred in relying on evidence which was inherently unreliable and did not meet the standard of proof required for conviction, that is, proof beyond reasonable doubt, and in this connection, you refer to an absence of medical reports or scientific evidence. The fourth ground is that the Trial Chamber, you say, erred in their application of Article 7(3) of the Statute, i.e., they erred in their finding that the appellant was in a position of superior responsibility, and as far as that ground is concerned, we would be grateful for your assistance as to whether you're saying that this was an error of fact or an error of law or both, and perhaps you could clarify that for us. Now, Mr. Joka, would you confirm that I have stated the grounds of appeal accurately, and if not, could you kindly indicate what the grounds are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, Your Honour, you have listed all the grounds of appeal which we indicated in our brief in which we challenge the guilty judgement regarding Count 10. Valuing your time and bearing in mind the fact that you have just said that you do not wish any repetitions to be made but merely any additional elaborations to be provided, in view of that, I would not have anything to add to what we have stated in our appeal regarding, first, discriminatory intent and, secondly, our claim that the violence committed was not sufficiently serious to warrant a condemnation. Those are the first two points that you have made. Third is the question of necessity or extreme necessity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's deal with the first two points, and you can assist us in some matters. There's a matter which I wish to raise in relation to the second of those grounds. You're saying, in effect, Mr. Joka, that the conduct for which the accused was convicted was not a serious violation of international humanitarian law as provided in Article 1; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you say that this is a point which you can take at this stage in the proceedings, although essentially it is a point against the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not challenging the jurisdiction of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whatever the merits of that are, supposing we did come to the conclusion that it was a point that you could take even at this stage of the proceedings, in an appeal against conviction, you're saying, are you, that the conduct which the Trial Chamber found proved, and for a moment assuming that that is what has been proved and that that conviction was correct, you're saying that it's not serious enough to come within the serious violations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. That is our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the position you held despite the fact that what the Trial Chamber found, and of course this is subject to your appeal, but assuming for a moment that it's correct -- we will have to decide whether it is or not -- that he was -- the accused, the appellant, was the warden of this detention centre; he mistreated, they say, the Trial Chamber found, at least two of the detainees; himself was involved directly in it; that as the warden he failed to prevent the mistreatment, violence to, and abuse of detainees; and that he was involved in the selection of detainees for trench digging and the use as human shields. That's the findings, if I've summarised them correctly. Are you saying that, particularly that latter finding, that he was involved in the selection of people and the conditions that existed at that time, trench digging and the use of human shields, so that is under the possibility of fire, that that's not a serious violation of International Humanitarian Law for a warden or a commander of a prison to be found guilty of?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to make a distinction. Such behaviour, conduct, is indeed a violation of humanitarian law, but our position is that this has not been proven, that facts have not been established that the appellant committed those acts and such conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I may have misread your pleading, but I don't remember that point being specifically pleaded. Mr. Joka, I can't remember you pleading that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we never claimed, nor gave any indication that such conduct, speaking in abstract terms, can be considered permissible and acceptable; on the contrary. If I may add, Your Honour. What was going on regarding human shields and trench digging, it is our submission and it was our position that this was outside the jurisdiction of the appellant. This was something carried out by the military police and under its control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, going on to the second ground -- I call it the second ground, but I may say it is attached, in light of what you just said -- you say that his conduct may have been justified by necessity. And as I understand your brief, you say that he acted out of necessity because he was thrown into a situation, after the conflict had begun, and he had to choose a lesser evil in what he had to do and, therefore, you say that the principle applies of exceptio causa necessitatio, not necessarily a principle which is familiar to common lawyers. You say, first of all, that that provides a defence to him. How do you explain that? You said you would expand on it and perhaps you'd do that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to try to provide a general framework. We lawyers were educated in the civil law system and as such, we have certain philosophies which we apply more or less automatically. Within that context, we offered, as a possible topic of discussion, that certain acts committed by the appellant were done so because he was in a situation of extreme necessity. What we implied under extreme necessity was summarised by you quite accurately a moment ago. We didn't claim extreme necessity as a defence in the course of the proceedings in view of the system in which we were educated and which we are working, because it is not customary in a common-law system, nor would it be right for us to lecture the Tribunal. That would be pretentious on our part. We just wished to highlight the facts to which the Tribunal will apply the law. We realised that according to the Rules of this Tribunal, there are only two defences, the alibi of defence or the alibi of limited mental capacity, and neither of these applied to our case. So we didn't think it necessary to use extreme necessity from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Joka, let me just understand. You're not saying that those are the only two defences which are open to an accused before this Tribunal, are you? They are defences to which particular rules apply, rules about disclosure, but an accused is free, of course, to raise any defence that he may legally raise and one which is relevant. You understand that, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Maybe I don't quite understand what is expected of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the point which has been made is that you didn't raise this defence before the Trial Chamber. You are raising it now. You're saying that it's a defence, that the accused acted out of necessity. The common lawyers might talk of duress, if you follow that. But how is it right for you to raise it on appeal when you didn't raise it before the Trial Chamber? Do you understand the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. Perhaps we expected the Trial Chamber would itself take that into consideration. Since they didn't do that, we thought it necessary to draw attention to this possibility in the appeals proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Joka, there is no material before the Trial Chamber from which any findings could have been made about that, is there? Surely you had an obligation as counsel to put the facts before the Trial Chamber from which it could have possibly made a finding of this defence of necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. We feel that we did provide the facts. That is our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where is the evidence? Can you just tell us what the evidence is so then we can understand what you're taking about? Where is the evidence of necessity?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt as to the period in which Zlatko Aleksovski was prison warden. There is also no dispute that before he took over, a certain number of detainees were already there. So as you yourself, Your Honour, mentioned, he found himself in a certain situation, and it is our submission that being in such a terrible situation, that this question of a lesser evil could be accepted, and in that sense, also the question of necessity, only insofar as that goes, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt so that we have it. I summarise what I understood your brief to say, and you are saying, are you, that from those matters which you say were part of the evidence, the Trial Chamber should have inferred or concluded that there was a defence of necessity open to your client? That's the way you put it, I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is our position that the Trial Chamber could have but need not have taken that into consideration. But if it felt that there were elements in support of such an inference, it should have done that. But, Mr. President, with your leave, let me say extreme necessity is not a crucial grounds of our appeal, if that is helpful in any sense in providing an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we leave that defence of extreme necessity, which you're now saying is not crucial to your appeal, I just want to be clear. Does the defence of necessity, if we are to accept it, does it go to the manner in which the accused treated the detainees or just the fact of detention? Because if you recall, the accused was found guilty of the manner in which he treated the detainees inside the prison and also allowing them to be -- selecting them for work outside the prison. So is the defence of necessity going to the fact of detention only, or to the manner in which the accused treated the detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the fact of detention, you probably mean the conditions of detention. I'm asking you so that I can give you a precise answer. In that case, it applies only to the treatment of prisoners, the latter point you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: By the accused, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Joka, in explaining the defence of necessity as you understand it, you said the accused chose a lesser evil, presumably as against the greater evil, but wouldn't it be open to him to have chosen no evil at all? Wouldn't that have been an option to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I don't know how to answer that question. That is a question of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The point, really, is that he had an option, and if he had an option, I don't see how necessity could apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are entering the sphere of hypotheses. He certainly couldn't have released the people, he couldn't have let them free. If he could have helped them in other ways, I don't know, that's a question of fact. We are just comparing the evil committed with a lesser evil. Radical solutions in that generalised madness were not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the more crucial grounds, as you call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may follow the order that you have suggested, Your Honour. As a fourth [sic] ground of appeal, which we discuss in our appeal brief, we claim that the conclusion is wrong because the evidence is not reliable beyond any reasonable doubt, that the treatment of detainees was such that resulted in certain bodily injury. We elaborated those points in detail saying what we meant by harm to body, how serious that injury must be and what the intention behind it must be. As far as I understand, maybe there is some doubt as to the question of evidence, that is, the medical documents and reports, or some other objective corroboration of the injuries sustained. That is how I understood your summary, Your Honour. In our appeal brief, we set out those grounds. May I just add that such a position of the Defence is also the consequence of the legal system we come from, and I think this is something that cannot be ignored, for the simple reason that everything relates to a state that fell apart, one could go further and say the whole of the Balkans, where relations are different and the philosophy and law is different than it is in Western Europe. It is difficult to make comparisons in the consciousness of an average Muslim man or a Croat man from Busovaca with an average person living in Lyon, for instance, France. The level of consciousness is quite different. Mentality, traditions are different. We cannot escape from our own traditions, nor are we trying to do that, nor can we ignore our legal system. Therefore, when we underline this point, that we feel that some objective evidence was needed to corroborate serious injuries sustained by those detainees, we do so because that is how we were trained and we are convinced that something that can be verified must be verified. To be more specific, in the case of injuries, this was left to each of the victims to tell the truth or not. It is up to His Honour. But there was a possibility to verify those things because there were medical centres, there were medical reports. We said all this in the course of our case, and that is why we feel that the evidence was not reliable beyond reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, that was Ground 3. You said Ground 4, but it was Ground 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The issue there is a matter for the Trial Chamber, is it not? They saw and heard the witnesses. It was for them to decide whether they were truthful witnesses and accurate witnesses. Therefore, if a witness said he was injured in a particular way, is there any reason -- if the Trial Chamber finds that he's telling the truth, he's accurate, isn't that sufficient evidence that he did sustain the injuries?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the Defence is that it is not. Allow me to make a comparison. Regardless of where a murder has occurred, a post-mortem will be carried out, some objective evidence must be provided, and there is a possibility to establish in an objective manner whether somebody sustained physical injury. We're not talking about mental harm, we're talking about bodily injury, serious bodily injury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Unless there's anything else you would like to add, perhaps you can deal with the next ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next ground was the question of superior responsibility, was it not? To be quite frank, I don't know what I could add to what we have already stated in our written brief. I think that our position is stated clearly. You asked whether it was an error of law or an error of fact. In answer to that, one must consider the relationship between the prison warden, a civilian, and the guards who were members of the military police, and his competencies in relation to them, those are facts. As to whether, in view of those facts, the law was properly applied, it is, of course, up to you to say and to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything you want to add, Mr. Joka? Is there anything you want to add to your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have nothing to add to the arguments presented in our appeals brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have those arguments and, of course, we will consider them in due course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Yapa, it may be that we can deal fairly briefly with these matters in the light of the brief arguments that we've heard. I don't think we need trouble you certainly on the first ground since no additional argument has been added. As to the other three grounds, there has been some matter on Ground 2; Ground 3 appears to be a straightforward matter of whether we think it right that the Trial Chamber were right in accepting the evidence or not in the form in which it was put before them; Ground 4, I don't think very much has been added to what we knew from the written submissions. But if there's anything you would like to add on Grounds 2, 3, and 4, perhaps you could do that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. In fact, when the appeal brief of my learned friend was received by us, on the ground of necessity, I mean no disrespect to my learned friend, we had certain difficulties in understanding as to what actually the Defence was speaking of. As Your Honour was pleased to ask him for an explanation to the defence of necessity, it appears that there isn't anything further that has to be added to whatever has been stated in the appeals brief and in the subsequent filings. We have, in our response, tried our best, as far as possible, to provide a comprehensive response to the appeal made by the appellant. I do not have anything further to add to the submissions that have been made. If Your Honours are inclined, if it is necessary for Your Honours' consideration, on the ground of necessity that has been raised, it may be possible to make further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's not much which you can assist us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll turn next to the Prosecution appeal. Mr. Yapa, we will hear your submissions. Again if you could bear in mind that we have had the written submissions for some time, and not go over them again, please. I know you won't. Part of your appeal is an appeal against sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you deal with that, I would be grateful if you would help us by pointing out precisely what it is you say -- what conduct you say that the accused was sentenced for. I have summarised it and, of course, we have read the judgement, but I think it's important, if we are to reconsider the sentence, we know precisely what it is that we have to pass sentence upon and to make sure there's no dispute about it. And I will give the appellant, obviously, the opportunity to respond to what you say the conduct is for which the appellant has been sentenced, but you will come to that, of course, in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we will hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the appeal by the Prosecutor, I intended to, at the commencement, make certain introductory remarks on the appeal made by us, but it appears that at the present moment, in the context of the proceedings now taking place, it may not be necessary for me to refer to all the items that I proposed to refer to. We have appealed on three grounds before Your Honours. They deal with -- the first ground of appeal is concerning the finding that it had not been proved that the victims were protected persons. It is our submission that the Trial Chamber erred in its judgement in deciding that Article 2 of the Statute was inapplicable because the Bosnian Muslims who were held in the Kaonik prison between January 1993 and the end of May 1993 were not protected persons within the meaning of Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions. This will be a ground of appeal on a matter of law, which will come under Article 25(1)(a) of the Statute. The second ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred in holding that the accused did not incur responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute for mistreatment suffered by the detainees outside the Kaonik prison compound. This ground of appeal may be identified as one of mixed question of law and fact. I say so because it is our submission that the Trial Chamber made a factual error in finding that the Prosecution had not claimed that the appellant was liable under Article 7(1) for mistreatment of the prisoners outside the prison other than their use as trench diggers and human shields. Further, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber erred in law in holding that the accused appellant did not incur responsibility on the basis of Article 7(1) for his participation in the mistreatment that the prisoners suffered while outside the prison compound. The third matter is the matter -- Your Honour, the precedent referred to is on the question of sentence. It is our position that the Trial Chamber erred in sentencing the accused to a term of two and a half years imprisonment. These grounds of appeal will be referred to and explained as we proceed. Your Honours' court has had occasion to pronounce on the function of the Appeals Chamber when it exercises it's appellant jurisdiction. In the Tadic decision, it was held that the jurisdiction of the Appeals Chamber was of a corrective nature, and as far as the Statute of the Tribunal is concerned, an appeal before Your Honours' court did not involve a trial de novo. We are mindful of the principle that we, as the appealing party, bear the burden of establishing the grounds of appeal we urge before Your Honours' court. It is for us to satisfy Your Honours that there is an error of law invalidating the decision or that there is an error of fact resulting in a miscarriage of justice. In the appeal brief of the Prosecution, we have made certain submissions on the nature of the standard that an appeal party must satisfy before the Appeals Chamber. Perhaps the subject needs further elucidation. On the premise that there is a standard that should be achieved and established on the first ground as stipulated in Article 25(1)(a), we illustrate two ways in which the errors of law may occur. Firstly, in regard to the substantive law and, secondly, in respect of the exercise of judicial discretion. On the first category, it is our submission that the Appeals Chamber has the authority to review the question or the matter of law, sitting as an appellate body. Of course, it is not to say that the Appeals Chamber acts oblivious of the judgement on the matter, by the Trial Chamber. It is for the parties seeking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is for the party seeking to appeal on a matter of law to satisfy the Appeals Chamber that the Trial Chamber has erred in law. On the question of the manner of exercising judicial discretion, our submission is not that the Appeals Chamber could substitute its will for that of the Trial Chamber. What is of necessity is that it has to be shown that the Trial Chamber abused its discretion, thereby causing prejudice to the appellant. For the purposes of the submission, we have identified certain situations typifying the exercise of judicial discretion by a Trial Chamber. It is our submission that in the absence of objection taken at the relevant time in the Trial Chamber in the proper manner, a party is not entitled to seek -- to seek to appeal upon that ground. On the second broad category of grounds of appeal, namely the ground of appeal under Article 25(1)(b), we make reference to two ways in which errors of fact may arise. The first is when additional evidence is available to show that an error of fact has occurred. It may be said that this situation does not strictly fall within the area of error of fact for the reason that the decision of the Trial Chamber was on the basis of the facts available at that time. The second type of error, error of fact, is that that is apparent on the face of the record. In the Tadic appeal decision, Your Honours' court set down a standard to be used in construing an issue of error of fact. It is very clearly stated that the task of hearing, examining, and weighing the evidence was a matter for the Trial Chamber. If the position is that the decision arrived at by the Trial Chamber could not reasonably have been arrived at by any reasonable person, then it is open to the Appeals Chamber to substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. This reasoning makes it clear that there can be differing opinions expressed by the trial Judges on the facts. The test of reasonableness is the test that is recognised by the Appeals Chamber. Although strictly not relevant to this part of the proceedings, there is one other matter I wish to refer to at this stage. Your Honours were pleased to, by the scheduling order of the 8th of December, 1999, make order on both parties to file additional submissions on the doctrine of stare decisis and the defence of necessity. On the defence of necessity, it may not be necessary for us to make submissions. I wish to, without going into detail, refer to the general position we take as regards stare decisis. We opted to use the term "precedent" on the basis that the principle known as stare decisis is not a general principle of law. The Appeals Chamber is the superior court or the superior court in this Tribunal or the final court in this Tribunal. We have, in our written submissions, stressed on certain reasons as to the desirability of the Appeals Chamber following the previous decisions of the Appeals Chamber on issues of law. I come next – to the question of the third ground of appeal. That is on the matter of sentence, which will be in detail presented by Mr. Norman Farrell. On the first two grounds, detailed submissions before Your Honours will be made by Mr. William Fenrick. I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I will speak to the first ground of appeal, and Mr. Farrell will address the other ones. I will bear in mind your admonition to be as brief as possible. I must, however, point out that at least to me, this is a particularly complicated issue and may take a little more time to address than some of the other ones. As its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution is appealing the finding by the majority of the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution had failed to prove that the Bosnian Muslim civilian detainees, who were the victims referred to in Counts 8 and 9 of the indictment, were protected persons under Article 2 of the Statute. To reach this finding, the majority of the Trial Chamber posed two questions and answered both of them in the negative. The two questions were, first, did the alleged mistreatment occur during an international armed conflict; and consequently, second, were the victims protected persons under the Fourth Geneva Convention, which is concerned with the protection of civilians. It is the submission of the Prosecution that the majority of the Trial Chamber erred because it applied the wrong test when endeavouring to answer each of the questions. If the correct tests had been applied to the facts, both of the questions would have been answered in the affirmative and the accused would have been convicted on Counts 8 and 9 of the indictment. Concerning the first question, which relates to the existence of an international armed conflict, it is the submission of the Prosecution that the proper test is the overall control test as set forth in the Tadic appeals judgement. As Your Honours will, of course, recollect, the incidents with which the Tadic Chambers were concerned occurred during the conflicts involving Bosnian government forces and Bosnian Serb forces. The Appeals Chamber, in that case, had to consider whether that particular conflict should be regarded as international because of the nature of the control exercised by Yugoslavia and its armed forces over the Bosnian Serbs and their armed forces. The test identified by the Appeals Chamber, which the Prosecution is referring to as the overall control test, is elaborated upon in paragraph 137 of the judgement, which states, in part, that control by a state over subordinate armed forces or militias or paramilitary units may be of an overall character and must comprise more than the mere provision of financial assistance or military equipment or training. This requirement, however, does not go so far as to include the issuing of specific orders by the state for its direction of each individual operation. Under international law, it is by no means necessary that the controlling authorities should plan all the operations of the units dependent on them, choose their targets, or give specific instructions concerning the conduct of military operations and any alleged violations of international humanitarian law. Now, as Your Honours will also recollect, of course, in the Tadic case, there were a variety of different tests put forward for specific situations or specific groups. It's our submission that the overall control test, which was one of three tests discussed, was the appropriate one both for determining the relationship between Yugoslavia and the Republika Srpska in the Tadic case and for assessing control, in this particular case, between Croatia and the Bosnian Croat entity and the Bosnian Croat forces. The majority of the Trial Chamber in this case failed to apply the overall control test and incorrectly decided that the Prosecution needed to demonstrate that Croatia had given a specific mandate or specific instructions to the Bosnian Croats with respect to the conflict in the Lasva Valley area, which is where, of course, the incidents related to this case occurred. It is submitted, this was the wrong question and imposed the wrong frame of reference for examining the evidence. The Prosecution submits that if the overall control test was applied correctly to the factual findings made by the Trial Chamber, it would have established that in the circumstances of the case, the Croatian authorities exercised overall control over the HVO in the first half of 1993. Further, it submits that in applying the test, one must have regard to the overall situation in Bosnia and Croatia. If Croatia exercised overall control, it did so for the entire HVO or the entire Bosnian Croat entity; it did not do so for parts of the HVO, in particular, parts of Bosnia. Second, if there is, in fact, or if the Court is convinced there is an international armed conflict between Bosnia and Croatia, the law for international armed conflict applies to all relations between Bosnia and Croatia, including the relations between the Bosnian Croats and Croatia, throughout the territory of both states not just to certain activities in particular areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the evidence -- supposing that we accepted your submission that the Trial Chamber applied the wrong test or the majority applied the wrong test, what, in brief, was the evidence which points to the fact that if they had applied the right test they would have come to the right conclusion? After all, I think they referred to overall control at one stage in the judgement, as I recollect it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, they certainly used the word, or the two words, and they may have used them more than once, but it was certainly -- first of all, you may recollect that this particular decision came out before the Tadic appeal decision was issued, and what had been discussed prior to that was a variety of tests related to the Nicaragua case as has been put forward in the Tadic trial decision and a variant of that was put forward in the Celebici decision, but it's our view that essentially what seemed to be focused on by the Trial Chamber was this concept of having orders being given to -- or a requirement, rather, that orders be given by Croatia to the Bosnian Croats in order for the test, whatever one called it, to be successfully applied. Our submission here is that we have a variety of things which are indicated in the evidence which would support effective application of the overall control test. One, in particular, would be the evidence of Croatian control over the Bosnian Croat entity. Now, we do have evidence, for example, which the Court accepted, that at a particular point in 1996, Mr. Tudjman was able to remove Mate Boban who was the head of the Bosnian Croat entity because he apparently was not following policies that Mr. Tudjman wished followed. If, as late as 1996, that kind of control could be exercised over the political leadership of the Bosnian Croats, and that is as late as 1996, it would be our submission that, if anything, you had a greater degree of control prior to that time. That linkage between the Bosnian Croat and the Croatian political entities would, from our perspective, be sufficient to establish overall control virtually by itself. We also, of course, have evidence which was accepted by the Court at the trial level that there were Bosnian Croatian -- excuse me, Croatian forces in Bosnia, uncontested evidence of that. That alone would not be sufficient, from the Prosecution's perspective, to establish that you had overall control over the Bosnian Croat forces. What we really have to do, we submit, or what the Court must be convinced of, is that there is a sufficient degree of control exercised over the Bosnian Croat military forces by the Croatian authorities, whatever they may be. Our submission is that there is ample evidence to support a conclusion of successful application of the overall control test with relation to the military aspect of things alone. What we have, the Trial Chamber -- well, perhaps if I might step back a bit. In the Tadic case, the way in which the various armed forces evolved was something like this: Initially, what we had was one state, Yugoslavia; one armed force, essentially the JNA. As things went along, as Bosnia broke away from Yugoslavia, of course the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia became the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In April of 1992, we have sort of roughly the date of creation of two armed forces where there had been one before. You get the creation of the VJ, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia armed forces, and the VRS, the Republika Srpska armed forces. But essentially it's the same armed force breaking into two. The Court in the Tadic appeals case essentially decided that this separate armed force, this VRS, was still under the overall control of Yugoslavia and that there were such links between the Yugoslav armed forces and the Republika Srpska armed forces that we could establish this overall control test and have an international armed conflict. We don't have precisely the same situation here. What we have is a different history, for starters, because, of course, Croatia didn't attempt to develop its own armed forces before, or at least not much before, it became or purported to become an independent state. So we don't have the equivalent of the JNA in Croatia as the Croatian armed forces. What we've got is the development of the HV which presumably is created roughly about the same time Croatia becomes an independent state. Shortly thereafter, we have the creation of Herceg-Bosna and we have Herceg-Bosna purporting to create its own armed forces, the HVO. We don't have this long history for the Croatian armed forces, but our submission is that there are very strong links between the two armed forces, that what we've got are, first of all, the existence of an integrated command structure which applies to the HVO and the HV both. In the particular exhibit referred to in the judgement, there is, of course, an indication that that applies to a particular period in 1992, but there's nothing that indicates it ever changes. In fact, it depends, I suppose, on what reading one gives to a variety of these documents. Our submission is you've got a joint command structure; you've got a lot of officers from the HV going to the HVO, in fact, manning a number of senior positions in the command structure; you've got the salaries of these officers continuing to be paid by the HV; we've got people moving back and forth between the two forces as if you, in fact, have a single armed force. They're moving back and forth and continuing to progress upwards in their careers. Essentially, it's our submission that not withstanding the fact there is not this prior history, as there could only be with the JNA, where the JNA splits up, what you've got here is essentially the creation of a combined structure over which Croatian military officers exercise substantial control. Armed forces, we can refer to it perhaps as some form of financial assistance, but armed forces are not in the habit of sending their officers on duty and continuing to be paid by them to fight other people's wars. They go to fight the wars of the country which employs them in the first place, and that country in this case is clearly Croatia. That's the fundamental way in which, it would be submitted by the Prosecution, Croatia exercises control over the HVO, and we submit that that, in fact, is sufficient, Your Honour. Now, I don't know if there are particular other points that you'd like referred to in connection with the overall control test. If we -- well, perhaps if I might conclude in connection with the overall control. Once again, as I move back to the beginning of my oral -- our oral submission, the point is that if there's overall control for part of the HV -- excuse me, the HVO, there's overall control for all of the HVO. This is not something where we've got bits and pieces, and there is enough evidence before -- or there was enough evidence before the Trial Chamber to establish this high degree of both military control by the HV over the HVO, because of the continued movement of officers, the integrated command structure, the continued payment of a large number of people, and a variety of other things that are mentioned in the brief of the Prosecution, and there is also this high degree of political control evidenced by the ability of then President Tudjman to remove Mate Boban, in particular, from the senior position in Herceg-Bosna. Now, if one accepts that this overall control test has been successfully met, then whether or not there is an armed conflict going on between Croatian troops as such, the HV and the ABiH, the army of Bosnia, we still have an international armed conflict because Croatia exercises -- provided you've got an armed conflict between Bosnia and the Bosnian Croats, if the Croats exercise overall control over Herceg-Bosna, then you've got an international armed conflict. To have an international armed conflict, we don't need to have fighting between the HV and the ABiH. The second question posed by the Trial Chamber in trying to determine whether or not the victims were protected persons is, in fact, if we take it as established that what we have is an international armed conflict in being between Croatia and Bosnia, then is the victim group, in this particular case, entitled protected persons status under Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions -- excuse me, under -- well, yes, entitled protected person status under Article 2 of our Statute. Now, under the Geneva Conventions, first of all, the victim group here is a group of Bosnian Muslim civilian detainees. The only possible Geneva Convention that they could have protected persons status under is the Fourth Geneva Convention which is concerned with the protection of civilian persons. If they are to be protected persons under the Fourth Convention, then Article 4 of the Fourth Convention defines protected persons, in part, as those who are "in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power of which they are not nationals." Now, what happened in this particular case is the Trial Chamber said, "Well, what we've got are Bosnian Muslim civilian detainees who have got Bosnian nationality, who are in a camp controlled by Bosnian Croats who may or may" -- some of them may or may not have Croatian citizenship because of Croatian legislation, but certainly it was not proved in court that they were Croatian citizens. The Court then concluded, "Well, you have Bosnians in the hands of Bosnians and, therefore, they were not protected persons, the victims were not protected persons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At first blush, an attractive proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, but not at second blush, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Because if the first threshold has been crossed and what you have is an international armed conflict -- if there is no international armed conflict, this argument doesn't work, but if there is an international armed conflict, then what happens is you've only got two parties to the international armed conflict, two things that are states. On the one side, what you've got is Bosnia; on the other side, what you've got is Croatia. You don't have a Bosnian Croat entity. That Bosnian Croat entity, whatever it is, is assimilated to or linked under or scooped up with Croatia. And notwithstanding the fact that, technically speaking, you may have the victim group in the hands of people who could be regarded as Bosnian Croats, when you interpret the Geneva Conventions even in the strictest sense, it would be our submission that those particular victims are in the hands of Croatia and couldn't possibly be in the hands of anybody else. There are two choices, and the two choices are Bosnia and Croatia, and they certainly aren't in the hands of Bosnia. Bosnia didn't put them in the detention facility. Bosnia didn't control their conditions of contention. Bosnia didn't decide that they were going to be released. The only state that's there, and it is a state, must be a state that's responsible for these people in detention, the only possible state is Croatia. So if we get over the overall control test, then the victims here are in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power, and that is Croatia, of which they are not nationals. It's submitted, although, frankly, it's not necessary to establish the protected person's status in this case, that if one has regard to the Tadic Appeals Chamber decision, they, in fact, tended to adopt a broader scope or a broader application of Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions, and they talked in terms of sort of ethnic allegiance, and they were talking in terms of, say -- well, for example, if you have, and this is not what we have here, but if what you had was a camp where you had the Bosnian authorities having Bosnian Croats in custody, the fact that the Bosnian Croats may have some allegiance to Croatia may also entitle them to protected people status, but that's not what we've got here. What we've got is in the hands of a party to the conflict or occupying power, the only possible party to the conflict or occupying power, if the overall control test applies, that is Croatia, and that meets the criteria for protected persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that's the way you put it in this case. You're not going to rely on the Tadic argument. Yours is a more straightforward one, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. In fact, the Tadic argument is, strictly speaking, not relevant here, Your Honours. The only way in which it fits in, after a fashion, is to counter an argument by the Defence that this is some form of unequal application of the law, that perhaps you might find yourself in a situation where we've got Bosnian Muslims detained by Bosnian Croats and applying a stricter interpretation. Those Bosnian Muslims would be regarded as protected persons, but you flip it around and you have Bosnian Croats in the hands of Bosnian Muslims, and then the Bosnian Croats wouldn't be protected persons. Now, that may be an end result if you apply the Geneva Conventions in a strict sense. If you adopt the Tadic approach that's not the result. Both groups are treated absolutely equally under the law. That, in substance, addresses the particular arguments that I was intending to make in this submission, Your Honours. We, of course, as a matter of remedies, would suggest that the criminal liability -- if one establishes this overall control test applies and the victims are protected persons, it's our submission that the criminal liability of the appellant on Counts 8 and 9 can be determined by the Appeals Chamber on the basis of the established factual findings of the Trial Chamber, and there's no need to refer the case back to the Trial Chamber for a redetermination of those counts. We would also submit, however, that if this is what is -- what your decision turns out to be, that of course for a matter of sentencing, the case should be sent back -- on these counts should be sent back to the Trial Chamber. That is the end of my submissions, Your Honour. I'm available for questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more convenient to deal with this question of sentence when we're dealing with the overall sentence question, but, Mr. Fenrick, of course, we haven't decided anything yet, but it may be convenient to have your submissions were we to be with you on reversing this verdict. Do you submit that it is necessary that the matter goes back to a Trial Chamber for re-sentencing, or we can deal with it? Again, I merely ask you because I want to know what your procedural submissions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Our recollection, Your Honours, is that in the Tadic case it, in fact, did go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is correct. It happened in Tadic, but in fact, it was at the submission of both parties that that should happen. It's now time for the adjournment. You may like to consider this. Is there any reason, you say, why we shouldn't deal with the matter ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If I may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Mr. Aleksovski, you are now under the authority of the Court. You are free to go during this adjournment, but would you please make sure you're back here in good time for half past 11, and the same will apply in the later adjournment. Very well. Half past 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, if you have an answer to the question I asked, and then Judge Robinson has a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honours. It would be our submission that unquestionably Your Honours have the authority to impose the sentence. We would suggest or submit that the issue be remitted back to the Trial Chamber so that the accused would have a right of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If, on the other hand, there was no increase in the sentence as a result of any sentence we might pass, then of course that would not be a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it were a concurrent sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fenrick, you are relying on the overall control test, but as I understand it, you're not suggesting that this Chamber should visit this matter afresh. You didn't, however, deal with the question whether this Chamber is bound to follow the decision of the Appeals Chamber on that matter. That's the stare decisis issue or the precedent issue, or more generally, simply just the question whether the Appeals Chamber is bound to follow a previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, in brief, recapitulate what's submitted in some of our briefs, and we don't argue that the Appeals Chamber is bound by a rule of stare decisis to apply its own prior decisions. Our submission would be that the Appeals Chamber should not depart from its own previous decisions unless it concludes that a prior decision was clearly erroneous and cannot stand. If at the time of the prior decision the law was uncertain, which may well have been the case in this particular instance, and it was open to different Judges to take a different view of the matter, the view that was taken by the Appeals Chamber in the prior decision should subsequently be accepted as the settled law. Departure from that decision might be justified, if it is plainly inconsistent, with settled legal principles if it was given per in curiam or other justifiable circumstances. However, the Prosecution submits it should certainly not be the general practice of the Tribunal to allow parties simply to relitigate matters which have already been settled in a previous decision of the Appeals Chamber. Here, we've got a decision in favour of the overall control test, admittedly to -- and it was applied to a different conflict, but we would submit that in this particular case, Your Honours should also adopt the overall control test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The position, as you have enunciated it, is generally the position followed in most common law countries. As I understand it, that's not the position followed in civil law countries. Why do you say that the Chamber, the Tribunal, should follow that particular approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly civil law countries don't adopt a rule of stare decisis or they don't use the expression, but it would be the submission of the Prosecution that, as a matter of simple judicial economy, most tribunals in most countries would be reluctant to review issues which they have already looked at in some detail in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll be addressing the second ground on behalf of the Prosecution which is the failure of the Trial Chamber to convict for the mistreatment which occurred outside the prison. That's not the trench-digging or the human shields. I'll also address the sentence appeal and hopefully address your questions, Your Honour, on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber. Regarding Ground 2, the liability under 7(1), direct participation, as they call it, for mistreatment outside the prison, the general position of the Prosecution is fairly straightforward and is set out in our brief. The Trial Chamber erred, in our submission, in finding that the accused was not liable for the mistreatment outside the prison carried on by the soldiers; that the Trial Chamber erred in its application of 7(1), and I'll specifically refer to the fact that they make reference to the necessity of direct participation; and, thirdly, that if you look at the facts as found by the Trial Chamber both with respect to the mental element and the act element, it's our submission that there can be no other conclusion, no other reasonable conclusion than he should have been convicted. I know it's clear to Your Honours, but there were three categories of conduct that were placed before the Trial Chamber which they addressed. The first was in relation to the human shields, that they were released from the prison through the assistance, by aiding and abetting by the appellant, for the use as human shields. The second was that they were released with the assistance of the appellant as an aider and abettor for the use as trench-diggers. The third basis which was addressed by the Trial Chamber, and it's the submission of the Prosecution that they should have found him guilty, is the mistreatment of the detainees for the abuse they suffered, that is, the physical abuse once they were outside of the prison. The focus, in our submission, is on at least apparently the actus reus. In paragraph 130 of the Trial Chamber's determination, they found that "It was not proved, however" -- I'm quoting: "It was not proved, however, that the accused participated directly in the mistreatment meted out to prisoners there," meaning outside during the time that they were trench-digging and they were human shields. It appears, therefore, that there is a lack of the act element, in other words, there wasn't the participation. It's respectfully submitted that the Trial Chamber was in error in that the actual facts that they found for both trench-digging and human shields, the act element, that is, is exactly the same, and that's the release of the detainees. The question of whether he knew they were being used for abuse, that's the secondary intent element, and that's found by the Trial Chamber. They find that he could not have been unaware that they were abused when they were returned recurringly. This isn't a case, in my submission, where they are released for a particular purpose, trench-digging or human shields, and while they're out there, randomly, unbeknownst to the appellant, they are beaten. This is a case where the Trial Chamber finds that on a recurring basis they are brought back and he's fully aware of the fact that they are beaten, and it's part of the process through which they are taken out. When you consider that they find that he has the mens rea or the mental element, we then go to the relevant findings of their findings with respect to the act element or the actus reus. In the Prosecution's submission, the actus reus for human shields and for trench-digging is actually the same for the beating. The actus reus is the encouragement, assistance for the aspect of their release with the knowledge that they are being released and that this is taking place. If you look at the facts found for the act element for human shields and trench-digging, you have his participation in the release, the designation and the selection sometimes when he's present, and he's almost always present upon their return to make sure that they return back. There's the recurring nature of the crimes, all three. The evidence is clear that the trench-digging is on a recurring basis. The witnesses testify that happens almost on a daily basis, the sending out for trench-digging, and they find that there were two occasions when the detainees were used for human shields. In fact, if you look at it in terms of the act element with respect to the human shields, the Trial Chamber finds, despite the Defence's position that the accused had no involvement in the human shields and had no knowledge in the human shields, if you recall the Defence position at trial, the Defence position with respect to the human shields issue was that they were not being used for human shields, or he didn't know they were being used for human shields. He acknowledges that they were released but not for human shields. The Trial Chamber finds that the act element is committed, just like trench-digging, by the release. That provides the assistance in that he could have taken action which might have prevented it. What they find for human shields, despite his denial of knowledge, is that in fact he must have known with respect to the incidents because of the acts of which he was aware, the conduct, the return. With respect, the human shields as found by the Trial Chamber was only on two occasions. The mistreatment outside the prison was a recurring event, according to the testimony of the witnesses, which appears to be accepted by the Trial Chamber, on a regular basis every time they went out, and the witnesses testified that they went out almost every single day. So if you accept the act element for the purposes of human shields, the offence of human shields for outrages upon personal dignity, it naturally follows that you must find that the act element is the same with respect to the mistreatment. It appears, and it's not clear, but it appears that the Trial Chamber takes the position that since he wasn't directly participating in the issue regarding the mistreatment, he can't be found guilty. Now, with respect, it's unclear what the Trial Chamber means. If what they mean by "direct participation" is a form of principal or perpetrator, in other words, he didn't plan the beatings, they were something that took place outside of the prison after they left; he didn't order the beatings because the Trial Chamber finds that he has no control over the HVO soldiers, accepting that to be factually accepted by the Trial Chamber, direct participation in those forms is not the allegation that he should have been found guilty for, it's aiding and abetting. If, by what the Trial Chamber said is direct participation, if what they mean is 7(1) liability, in other words, it's just the way it's phrased --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My apologies to those who have to keep up. With respect to the second aspect of it, being if direct participation -- if the Trial Chamber means by "direct participation" 7(1) liability, if they mean that, then, with respect, they are in error because the facts that they find which are that he has the knowledge clearly and his acts, as in trench-digging and in human shields, facilitate the release, then there can be no other conclusion that he had the mens rea and the actus reus, the act and mental element, for the offence of mistreatment outside the prison and should have been convicted for outrages upon personal dignity for this category of conduct. That, in summary, is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I wonder if you can help me with this: There has to be a finding by the Trial Chamber of the mistreatment, and apart from the reference in paragraph 128 about "... he would have seen the marks of repeated abuse which was clearly visible on the prisoners upon their return ..." I cannot find any finding as to what that mistreatment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's a fair enough question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you see, there was a fundamental problem at the trial as to the way in which it was pleaded that you had an ambiguous statement as to whether you were relying upon beatings inside and outside or one or the other. The Trial Chamber, as you've pointed out, in fact, acknowledged that you were making an allegation of mistreatment outside the prison, but it's not clear from any finding they make and it's not clear from the indictment what the mistreatment was. You said that they have obviously accepted the testimony of some witnesses. We don't have that testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour. Just in response. There was a conclusive finding in the judgement, as you've indicated, that abuse took place outside the prison. There are references, and I'll give you the paragraph numbers, if I may. Paragraphs 116 and 117 of the judgement do not deal specifically with the abuse that took place outside the prison but it refers to the position of the Defence which is that there were exhibits submitted, 116 and 117 refer to Exhibit 22, I think it is. Exhibit 22 is the Defence Exhibit put forward to say that the appellant submitted a report to the authorities with respect to two killings that took place outside the prison. Now, my understanding from looking at the evidence is those killings took place on February the 7th, it's in the first period of detention. The Trial Chamber doesn't appear to distinguish which period he's speaking about in the passage you referred to, Your Honour. If it's found, and it's submitted that it is found, that these individuals were killed while they were out on trench-digging duty on February the 7th, the accused was found by -- the appellant was found by the Trial Chamber to have taken over responsibility, I think it is, January 23rd, and the testimony accepted by the Trial Chamber is that the abuse took place over a considerable period of time and was reoccurring. One can assume that the period of detention of the first period, which I understand went from January 23rd to February the 8th, that there was the sending them out for trench-digging during this period of time as a recurring basis. On that basis, he must have known that there was abuse taking place. My understanding from the exhibit, I stand to be corrected because I was trying to sort this out, is that the killings took place on February 7th, the day before the ultimate release of the detainees on February the 8th. So at that point in time, it would be the Prosecution's submission that certainly if there is knowledge found that they're recurring during this period and trench-digging does take place, then he certainly has at that point in time knowledge of one act which, we would submit, would constitute the aiding and abetting. Secondly, I'll refer you to paragraph 128 that you've referred to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That obviously refers to something more than killings; that refers to physical abuse to the prisoners which would have been clearly visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There seems to be no findings in the circumstances or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I just may refer to a few other matters, Your Honour. There is -- once again, it's not of great assistance, Your Honour, but under paragraph 224, once again, it's just a general finding, Your Honour, not a specific finding, and it's a short summary by the Trial Chamber of the evidence in relation to which this appellant can be found liable for. The sentence simply states, and I'm into the third sentence -- the third line down: "The state in which some of the detainees returned from digging trenches ..." So once again, Your Honour, that's the extent of the finding. If I may, the Prosecution relies on -- there were at least five witnesses, and I'll just read them into the record, if I may. Witness M, the transcript reference is 1431 to 1449, 1457 to 1462, and 1470 to 1481. Second witness is Witness L, 1378 to 1399. Third witness is witness O, 1576 to 1586. The fourth witness is Witness H, a transcript reference, 914 to 926. And the fifth is Witness B, transcript reference page 573 and pages 581 to 588. Most of these reference were attached to the closing brief in the annexes by the Prosecution, and in light -- and these witnesses speak of the abuse that took place during the time that they were out in the field doing trench digging. In light of the two very specific findings in paragraph 128 and paragraph 224 that the appellant must have known and that there was repeated abuse, the Prosecution would rely on the statements of these witnesses, which is uncontradicted and, in the Prosecution's submissions, by inference accepted by the Trial Chamber as being correct in light of their findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you understand that the Prosecution is seeking to make the accused or the appellant, as he now is, liable for the acts of others. Then, of course, the Prosecution asks the Chamber to impose a sentence in relation to that. We have to know what those acts are, and so far as I can see from the judgement, they are stated in the most general of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I can't dispute that, Your Honour. I can take it to its highest and indicate that in light of the fact that there was no contrary findings, all the testimony of the witnesses regarding the abuse was found by the Trial Chamber. All the testimony that we've referred to in those five witnesses and others appears to be the basis upon the finding. And the fact that the Trial Chamber -- I understand the predicament the Appeals Chamber is in, Your Honour, but the fact that the Trial Chamber makes findings of fact and then -- general findings of fact in respect of the abuse and concludes at that it's unnecessary to go into it because they find that he wasn't directly participating in the form that they find, shouldn't necessarily go to the detriment of the Prosecution when the Trial Chamber is in error, an in light of their general findings, we would submit that the evidence put forward in relation to the abuse has been accepted by the Trial Chamber and, therefore, is basis upon which we would submit that the finding of guilt should be made and the facts in relation to that should be relied on for sentence, but that's the highest I can put it, Your Honour. I appreciate your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. That being the case, those are essentially the submissions that I wanted to add in relation to the second ground of appeal. Subject to any other questions, I'll move on to the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Farrell, you can assist, at the outset, by ensuring that there is no dispute, and we have to be clear as to the what the accused is to be sentenced for and what the findings of the Trial Chamber were. It may be of assistance if I summarise the position as I understand it. Dealing with the liability under Article 7(1), the Trial Chamber found the accused guilty of aiding and abetting mistreatment. I'm using this in a general sense rather than a technical sense, because of course it's the effect we want of the crimes, the effect of them generally, not particularly their legal classification at this stage, which we need to consider. Aiding and abetting the mistreatment of several detainees during body searches on the 15th and 16th of April, and that included insults, threats, thefts, and assaults upon them. Next, ordering or instigating and abetting violence on two witnesses, L and M, when the accused was present, and ordered the guards to continue. And M's injuries included his fainting as a result of his being beaten; traces of blood in his urine; and was said, at the time of the trial, to still be suffering from back and chest pain. The next allegation or the next matter that was proved, rather, aiding and abetting the physical abuse of detainees. It was said to be frequent, day and night, near the appellant's office, but he did not stop it. And there were various injuries sustained by detainees, serious spinal injuries and a broken nose. There was psychological abuse, threats, direct threats to them. Next, and you can help me as to whether this is correctly defined, aiding and abetting the mistreatment of detainees during interrogations. This involved a number of detainees. I don't think the number was specified, but they were detainees who had escaped and were interrogated by the accused. Next dealing with the acts outside the prison, in which the accused was found guilty of aiding and abetting the use of detainees as human shields and for trench digging. This is by taking part in designating the detainees for trench digging, not preventing the HVO soldiers coming to get the detainees and participating in picking them out, and being present when detainees were taken to serve as human shields and thereby showing his approval of the practice. Under Article 7(3), he was found to be liable as superior -- that is, the warden of the prison -- for the crimes committed by the guards in the prison, because he took no measures to prevent the crimes being committed. Now, that is a summary of the matters for which he was sentenced, as I understand it, and for which we have to reconsider the sentence according to your appeal. Now, if there are any other matters which fall to be considered following the judgement, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In relation to the facts that you've set out, I've gone through the list of everything that I've noted and, in fact, you've identified everything. There is only one reference in addition. It's not that serious. It's just the psychological violence. You mentioned it already. It's just one of the categories of conduct in that the Trial Chamber found that there was, on occasion, a number of times where the accused, as obviously an aider and abettor, permitted the recording of songs and the playing of screams over the loudspeaker of detainees as they were being beaten in the night. That's just one element of psychological violence to the other detainees who had to listen to it. But other than that, in relation to both the 7(1) and 7(3), Your Honour, I have nothing to add in relation to the facts themselves as found by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. And, of course, it appears that it was not possible to quantify the number of detainees that were involved in a number of these matters, such as how many were affected by the crimes. This was a prison in which there were numerous crimes, the Trial Chamber finding that, for instance, the psychological abuse, the physical abuse, was going on day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct, and that would be our submission. As of an ongoing nature, the quantification is not done in a specific sense by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Essentially, I note, first of all, that the Prosecution put a fairly lengthy brief in on the issue of sentencing. It's not my intention in anyway to restate that. I would note at the outset, though, that it doesn't appear in the response by the appellant accused that he addresses the issue of sentencing in his response brief. He simply indicates that obviously he opposes the Prosecution's position, and he takes the alternative position that since he's obviously appealing and seeking a remedy of acquittal, that the appellant shouldn't have been sentenced in any event. In light of that, it's unclear what issues are in dispute in relation to the Prosecution's submissions by the Defence, except for all of them. In that regard, if there's anything that's raised just as a procedural matter during my colleague's reply, counsel for the appellant, I may note that it may be addressed in our reply, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, would it be simplest to hear what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- what the appellant has to say on these matters? We have, as you rightly say, your written submissions. Unless there's anything in particular you want to refer to, it may be more convenient to deal with it in that way and, of course, you could rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There are only two issues, Your Honour, and I'll just note them. The first is that Prosecution wanted to apprise you of the fact that the Prosecution has taken the position in three matters which are coming before the Appeals Chamber, this case obviously, the case of Furundzija, and the case of Celebici, on the importance of establishing some principles of sentencing in relation to the Appeals Chamber. In all three briefs, similar submissions have been made and we will be making similar submissions with respect to the principles that are set out in the brief. So simply to inform you that this position of the necessity for specific sentencing principles is something that the Prosecution will be submitting in other matters. Of course, we're not asking that this Appeals Chamber go outside of the scope of the appeal that's presently before you or the facts that are before you, but just that there's some sentencing principles which are particularly applicable to this case, and it's the Prosecution's submissions that the Trial Chamber erred in relation to the application of those principles, and that's set out in the brief. The second point I wanted to bring to your attention, and this has nothing to do with the quantum, of course, if there's anything in reply I'll address that then, but the second thing is that at the time the Prosecution filed its submissions, the Appeals Chamber's decision on the sentencing judgement in Tadic had not been released. As a result, there are simply two issues that were raised in the Tadic decision that I wanted to take this moment to give you the Prosecution's position. In our brief, the Prosecution's brief presently before you in Aleksovski, we note the position in Furundzija and Celebici, that the paramount consideration or one of the strongest considerations on sentencing is deterrence, and the submissions are placed in the brief with respect to the significance of deterrence based primarily on our submission that the starting point of any sentence is the gravity of the offence. In the Tadic appeal judgement, you'll note that the Appeals Chamber dealt with this issue -- I don't have it in front of me, I'm sorry. In any event, the Appeals Chamber dealt with this issue, and in dealing with it, it found that deterrence should be not accorded undue prominence. In light of that, there seems to be a bit of a difference between our position on the appeal -- thank you to my colleagues. I'm sorry. Just for your reference, the discussion of the Appeals Chamber's judgement in the sentencing appeal in Tadic is paragraph 48. In that, the Appeals Chamber concludes that it does not dispute the relevance of deterrence or that it's legitimate, but that it must not be accorded undue prominence in the overall assessment of the sentences to be imposed. Just to clarify then the Prosecution's position, first of all, the Prosecution's position is that the Tadic decision, though obviously making this general statement, didn't enunciate any further on the extent to which deterrence is to be taken into consideration and what weight it is to be given. It doesn't mean that the Prosecution is now asking for a rehearing of that issue. Undoubtedly an unfit sentence can't be justified by too much emphasis on deterrence, and clearly the elements that we submit in our brief are the gravity and the circumstances of the accused.
