That's the starting point, but the Prosecution would note, in consideration of the Tadic decision regarding deterrence, that the general principles that are used in sentencing, at least in the common-law jurisdictions of which I'm aware, include other forms of sentencing and other means, release, and escorted temporary absence pass, probation, and also take into consideration principles such as rehabilitation or reintegration into the community. It is the submission of the Prosecution in the brief that those factors, although obviously relevant to the particular circumstances, the mitigating circumstances of the accused, are not that paramount before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's an entirely different position from the domestic jurisdiction. Not only are there no powers, the matters are irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Exactly. That's the point that the Prosecution wanted to make in relation to our submission on deterrence, that deterrence is, as a result of the objectives and purposes as found in the Tadic interlocutory decision, there's three purposes, and the second is to deter future violations. In light of the fact that other principles may not be particularly applicable, the Prosecution still stresses the importance of deterrence, though accepts the decision in Tadic which seems to say that it is not the sole or determining factor. Obviously, if undue prominence was the quality or characteristic to be given to the sentence, then this would mean imposing the highest sentence in every case regardless of the accused's personal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The relevance is to look at the gravity of the conduct which has been found and determine the sentence. Clearly, retribution plays a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There are a number of factors that are in their denunciation, as it may be called, in other systems and what are submitted in our brief. Of course, Your Honour, the educative and suppressive elements, the suppressive element is the actual deterrence, both specific deterrents with respect to this accused or the circumstances in which this accused found himself in and committed it, and general deterrence, which is to deter others who may be in like circumstances. And then what we submit in our brief to be the educative effect, which is the general revulsion of the International Community of this type of conduct and the necessity of indicating that this type of conduct is not acceptable. If I may, that leads to the second principle or finding in the Tadic appeal judgement that I just wanted to make a short submission on, if I may, and that's in relation to the determination of the role and the level of the commander in the broader conflict. Once again, the Tadic appeal judgement on sentencing refers to this at paragraphs 55 and 56 and concludes in paragraph 57 that the sentence should be reduced. The particular point that the Appeals Chamber appears to be making in this case is that you -- the Trial Chamber or in sentencing now as an Appeals Chamber yourself, have to adequately consider the need for sentences to reflect the relevant significance of the role of the appellant in the broader context of the conflict. And then they find in the case of Mr. Tadic that his level in the command structure, when compared to that of his superiors, in this case they refer to commanders or the architects of the strategy of ethnic cleansing was low, and this was one of the basis upon which they -- one of the basis, I'm sorry, upon which they reduced his sentence. The Prosecution's submission in this regard is essentially twofold. First of all, in an effort to recognise the necessity of gradation of sentences, the necessity of having a distribution depending on liability, it is respectfully submitted that the Appeals Chamber should not lose sight of the gravity of the crime. Simply trying to fit the matter within a proportional equal distribution may result in a sentence which is not fit to the crime which was committed, and the obvious example which we place in our brief is that if one commander directly participates in the killing of ten individuals and another directly participates in the killing of a hundred or is involved in a much wider campaign, in the Prosecution's submission, at some point in time, you can't distinguish between certain acts based on the level of the commander or the role. When the crime itself is so grave that if the commander is not at the highest level but has committed a number of crimes, then, in our submission, the sentence should reflect what would be the normal course in domestic jurisdiction that a murder is a murder, and that in this case, especially in terms of conflict, you can't diminish the value to the victim or the necessity of the gravity and deterrence of the sentence simply because there are other people who committed more than he has. That's inevitable in any armed conflict unless you're only going to prosecute the highest level. As well, it implies, of course, which is obvious, that the issue in relation to superior orders -- in other words, if you're going to diminish the sentence because the person was a bit less in terms of their role, this is one of the issues that goes under, just to take note of 7(3), command responsibility or, for example, superior orders where it's concluded that superior orders are no defence but may go on mitigation. When we're talking about the accused in this case, it's not a case of superior orders. The role in command as set out in Tadic, in our respectful submission, is not the issue here, and though the Trial Chamber in our case refers to the role of Mr. Aleksovski vis-à-vis the others who he was initially indicted, Kordic, which you're fully aware of, and others, was of a minor role. We're not seeking his sentence to be changed because of his role vis-à-vis the others that he was placed on the same indictment with. He is a commander in his own right. The Trial Chamber's finding that he was merely a tool of the broader plan to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley is not the basis of our appeal per se. He was not merely a tool when he was the commander himself and was the top ranking official in the prison which resulted in the others being permitted to do it. So if you're going to apply this role and level of command in the broader conflict, it's respectfully submitted that you have to take it into consideration in relation to the specific circumstances that take place. In that case, he is the commander in that case, and anything that takes place in the prison is his responsibility under 7(3) and cannot be diminished by the fact that he doesn't play a greater role vis-à-vis the Lasva Valley ethnic cleansing. That's our position with respect to Tadic, that his relationship vis-à-vis others obviously can't diminish the gravity of the offence for which he committed. The only other thing I'd note, just as a factual matter, the Trial Chamber finds that as a fact he had no role to play except for a limited role as an aider and abettor in human shields and trench-digging. This way he did facilitate the greater role but he was merely a tool. With respect, you'll note that the findings of fact by the Trial Chamber with respect to trench-digging specifically is not that he was merely a tool, and with respect, that was an error in the classification. The appellant clearly agreed with the trench-digging; in fact, his defence was that it was necessary and that all civilians of the area had to be involved in trench-digging, it was required by law, and that it was part of the defence at that point in time of the area under which the Bosnian Croats had control. So in that respect, he wasn't merely a tool, he was actually facilitating and was directly involved and approved of the use of detainees for trench-digging, despite the fact that he'd been told by the ECMM and the ICRC that it was contrary to international law, and this was for the purpose of something greater than just the scope under which he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not saying that we shouldn't follow Tadic on that question. What you're saying is that the factual situation is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Without trying to in any way backtrack, the submission is that the Appeals Chamber or the sentencing chamber cannot give too much weight to this concept of the broader role and the greater conflict. If it diminishes the gravity of the offence with which the accused is convicted, in an effort to try and determine the proper gradation of sentence which is understood because of the level of culpability of the individual accused who will come before the Tribunal, one can't diminish, as in this case, very serious crimes, involved directly and as a 7(3) commander, very serious crimes in sending people out to risk and for aiding and abetting in human shields and trench-digging, and just claiming that he was -- THE COURT REPORTER: Would you please slow down, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My apologies. I'll try and be a little slower as well for you, Judge Robinson. Thank you. In this regard, there's essentially two positions: One is that as a general principle, this can't outweigh the gravity of the crime, and the Appeals Chamber or the Trial Chamber shouldn't attempt to reach some type of gradation when the seriousness of the offence certainly in and of itself would require a greater sentence; and then the application of that principle to this case is the second point which I made and which Your Honour has noted. The last thing, Your Honour, is simply that the submissions with respect to the quantum are in the brief. It's seven years. In relation to other matters of sentence, for example, the Ground 2, which is if you find him guilty of mistreatment, the position obviously is the same, with respect to the significance, if necessary, of an appeal by the accused or by the Prosecution, for that matter, if you determine that the sentence is to be changed. I would just finally note that in the Tadic decision, it was sent back to the -- there wasn't any determination by the Appeals Chamber as to what the appropriate sentence would have been. It was sent back, deferred back or remitted back to the Trial Chamber. We note in that case that when it did come up on appeal, the Appeals Chamber did find a separate sentence than was submitted to by the Trial Chamber. So in that case, it did indirectly justify the necessity of having the benefit of the Trial Chamber's analysis of the sentence and the sentence which, as we know, was subsequently varied on appeal. Those are my submissions, subject to any questions. I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Joka, we will hear you now in response to the Prosecution, if you'd like to deal with all three grounds of appeal. I should add that we've seen what you've written in response, of course. It's merely if there's anything you would like to add, particularly in relation to anything which has been said today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honours. We now have three points that are being mentioned: First, the protected persons grounds, and that is the question of whether there was the existence or not of an international armed conflict; that is to say, whether conditions existed which could be reviewed and the decision as to guilty or not guilty and the two points for which the appellant was acquitted; that is one question. The other one was the abuse of prisoners outside Kaonik camp. The third question or grounds is a balancing out or determination of sentence. So I'd like to say a few words on these points. Let me say at the outset, before I present our own views with regard to protected persons and international conflicts, that I have perhaps not been understood. Some things that I have heard today are not quite clear to me, with all due respect to everything that my learned colleagues have stated so far. So either I did not understand them correctly or there is some lack of logic in what they have said. This, just by way of an introduction. We heard today in the arguments put forward, that is to say, the Tudjman-Boban relationship of 1996 was mentioned, for example; that is to say, something about which we have seen not a single piece of evidence and which is outside this court case in general. It was stated that overall control over a portion of the HVO means that there was overall control over the entire HVO. So this has been turned upside down, it appears to me, and that is not the way we should be looking at it. We cannot conclude from this little piece that overall control existed and go on to claim the bigger. We also heard mention of the political supervision of Tudjman/Boban. We're not dealing with politics here and that aspect of it. We also heard that Croatia was the occupying force and that it decided on the regime that held true in the prison and whether the prisoners should be released or not. This is something that I'm hearing for the first time here today. I have seen no evidence or proof in the course of these proceedings as to anything of that kind, nor was it brought up against the accused. Finally, something that I feel to be particularly important is something that we had occasion to hear here today, that the Tadic case is irrelevant to this particular case, the Aleksovski trial. Now, if the Tadic case is irrelevant to these particular proceedings, how can we then keep referring to it, and what I'm going to say now applies to each of the individual points. We keep appealing, that is to say, the learned members of the Prosecution keep referring back to the Tadic case and they claim that the Trial Chamber erred, forgetting that the decision in the Tadic case was brought subsequently, after the first sentencing and judgement was made. So how could the Chamber err if something did not exist when it did its work? With your permission, I should like now to say a few words about the international conflict which, according to our tribunal, is the crux of the whole problem and the basic element upon which we built up our defence case with relation to points 8 and 9, Counts 8 and 9. It is a combination of fact and law. First, I should like to stress that we cannot deliberate about Bosnia-Herzegovina as being a unified, united state and country. Bosnia is sort of a melting pot which brings together the passions of three nations in which territory has been divided and in which everybody is against everybody else, which brings us to the ultimate absurdity in the Cazinska Krajina region where the Muslims fought against the Muslims. I bring this up by way of illustration, and if we applied the standards brought up by the Prosecution, then that conflict too should be deemed to be an international conflict as well, I suppose. However, we're not discussing Bosnia now, we're discussing the Lasva River Valley, which is a more narrow territory. It is an enclave inhabited by Croats surrounded by Muslims. It is quite a different environment to the Cazinska Krajina region or the Croats in Posavina, so on and so forth. There are quite different interests there. It would be illusory even to imagine that people and the political leadership of this one enclave could have the idea that they would live in some other state, when de facto there was no possibility for this because they were living in an encirclement, they were living in the centre of a sort of melting pot from which they cannot emerge. Furthermore, I should like to enumerate, just in the form of thesis, not to take too much of your time, what I wish to say; namely, we heard about the HVO units in the enclave. There has been not a single piece of evidence presented, no proof at all that in the Lasva River Valley the presence of HV units were determined. Furthermore, another question was raised previously and was brought up again today. The Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Muslims quite obviously are citizens of one and the same state, and there the provisions and laws are quite clear and apply to one and all. All of them are citizens of the same state, and if we add to this the fact that a portion, or more exactly point 2 of the Fourth Geneva Convention which was not quoted, then this leads us on to another conclusion. My learned colleague quoted point 1 relating to protected persons, and in point 2, the following is stated: "We shall not consider persons to be protected persons for as long as the state of which they are citizens have regular diplomatic representations in the state in which the authorities prevail." So even if we were to leave behind the criteria that they are citizens of one and the same state, in fact, we at the same time have the fact that between Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are permanent diplomatic relations and that there are diplomatic offices of Bosnia in Zagreb, for example. There, the provisions are quite clear, and I don't know whether we can understand it extensively. There is evidence which I cannot quote because of its status and which was point D, Exhibit 29A and B and Exhibit D30 to D34, those exhibits which also speak along those lines. Finally, as we're discussing this unfortunate international conflict, a letter by the authorised representative of the Muslims in the United Nations, Mr. Sacirbey, who writes that in this concrete case, that is to say, in the Lasva River Valley, which is precisely the locality in which the events took place that we're discussing here today, that it was a conflict between local leaders, and I quote: "Conflict between local leaders in the Lasva River Valley," that is, D13, Exhibit D13. I should like you to bear in mind that that letter was written on the 21st of April, 1993, and that is exactly five days after Ahmici. Ahmici, as far as I know, is the pivotal point, and several cases relate to that particular point. That is what I wanted to say with respect to the international conflict. I say they are theses that I have put forward. Now, as far as the overall control test is concerned, if we said that it was used in the Tadic trial and we say that the Tadic trial is not relevant for our trial, for our case, why, then, should we deliberate it, because the situations are entirely different; that is, it is impossible to draw any parallel which we have done in tabula, we have shown this in tabula form --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Joka, I think to be fair to the Prosecution, when they referred to the Tadic trial as not being relevant, it was in relation to a specific point. The specific point, as I remember it, was the question of allegiance on the basis of ethnicity. I don't think it was being said that the Tadic trial was not relevant in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, what the Prosecution was saying was that the overall control test was the one which should be applied. So you can direct your submissions to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall take that into account and your cautions. I have misunderstood it then. But as we're speaking about the overall control test, I can only reiterate that I consider that there are no conditions -- that the conditions do not exist for this overall control test to be applied for the simple reason that these are two diametrically opposite situations. I should like, with your permission, now to say two or three words about the abuse of prisoners outside Kaonik camp, unless you have some questions with regard to the first portion. Thank you. Well, we have these unfortunate human shields, this trench-digging, and the abuse of people on the ground. Actually, our position is essentially identical to the one taken up by the Trial Chamber, and that is that Zlatko Aleksovski, that is to say, that there is no evidence to show that Zlatko Aleksovski had effective control over HVO soldiers and members of the military police; that is to say, control over those individuals who took these people out of the camp and took them off, regardless of the fact that we can claim that it was their forced labour duty or assignment or anything like that, we can leave that aside for the moment. What I'm saying is that it has been objectively ascertained that he did not have the possibility of controlling those individuals. The fact that the killing of two individuals took place and that he took certain steps, that shows something quite the opposite; that is to say, that when he had knowledge of the fact that something happened which should not have happened, he did, indeed, undertake something that was under his competence, and that is that he informed the investigating centre of the competent court of law and that he filed a criminal report. We know that from the facts as they stand; I need not repeat that. To deduce from this, as the Prosecution has been doing, that if he knew about this, he must necessarily have known about the abuse on the ground, I think is rather unsubstantiated and all the more so because evidence has not been provided from which we could ascertain the number of abused individuals, who these individuals were, and in what way they were abused. We listened to the testimony of people who were outside the camp and got different statements. I don't want to repeat them, but some people said they were kicked and some people said quite the reverse, that an HVO soldier had given them a jacket to keep them warm, or things like that. So this is a question of the evidence provided and the weight, weighing the evidence, putting it in the balance. As far as the third ground is concerned, the circumstances in balancing out the sentence and determining sentence, with regard to the conduct for which he was found guilty, Your Honours, we did not intentionally wish to state our views because it is our position that the appellant should be acquitted, and we do not feel that it would be proper or morally in order, as is frequently the case, to plead this if he is pronounced guilty, that the following should be taken into consideration. We didn't do that on purpose. But I should like to say now that it is contrary to the legal standards adopted to pitch a sentence, always maintaining a higher upper-most maximum, if I have understood my learned colleagues correctly. A sentence or judgement cannot be a memento for other cases or a caution to others which are being tried so judiciously, and I think that this Trial Chamber will have, if it assesses that the sentence should be modified either up or down, some usual standards. Of course, we must discuss prevention, special prevention with respect to the perpetrator, or a deterrence, as it has been termed - general prevention, general deterrence and how it will affect potential perpetrators - but we must not forget individualisation of sentences. You cannot have one in the same sentence for everyone. Well, that is all I have to say for the moment. Thank you. If there are any additional questions, I shall be happy to address them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Joka. We will now consider this matter, unless there's anything -- is there anything anybody wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: There are a few matters which we would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. In connection with the Prosecution's first ground of appeal, quite obviously the Tadic appeal decision was issued after the Aleksovski trial decision; however, it's the submission of the Prosecution that that is not relevant. Second, from the Prosecution's point of view, no, we are not talking about the Lasva River Valley only, we are talking about events throughout Bosnia and, for that matter, Croatia to the extent they are relevant. Third, in connection with the relationship between President Tudjman and Mr. Boban and the question of command generally, we would submit that a review of paragraphs 24 to 27 of the majority decision concerning Article 2, and in particular, a look at the footnotes in the documents referred to therein might be of assistance. Last of all, concerning the "diplomatic relations" issue, the Prosecution would refer to the paragraph that was referred to by the appellant, and I would recite that particular paragraph or part of it, and it says, among other things: "Nationals of a co-belligerent state shall not be regarded as protected persons while the state of which they are nationals has normal diplomatic representation in the state in whose hands they are." We are not talking about a co-belligerent state in this particular context. "Co-belligerent" doesn't mean the two sides fighting each other, it means people on the same side. That's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Farrell, is there anything you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Just one minor point, with your indulgence. In response to my learned colleague's comments that the abuse -- knowledge of the abuse by the accused was unsubstantiated and the reference to the two killings, I'd just ask if it is relevant, that you refer to paragraph 33, where at trial the Defence concedes, in fact, that they -- that there was knowledge that the appellant was aware that there was occasional mistreatment by the HVO during trench digging. In addition, the Defence concedes that in one instance, two internees were actually killed. For clarification purposes, there was a concession at trial not only with respect to the two who were killed, which he's relying on, but with respect to occasional mistreatment. That's all I wanted to bring to your attention. Thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll rise to consider what course we'll take. We'll sit again in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appellant's appeal against conviction is dismissed; reasons will be given in a written judgement in due course. We reserve judgement on the Prosecution appeal against acquittal, that is Grounds 1 and 2, but we allow the Prosecution appeal against sentence, that is Ground 3. That requires us to pronounce a revised sentence. We shall not do that today but shall consider sentence. Accordingly, the appellant must now remain in custody until such time as revised sentence is pronounced. We will notify, in due course, as to a date for the pronunciation of judgement and sentence. That concludes this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please. Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rise.
